unit.title: In the Classroom: En el Salón de Clases

lesson.title: ¿Qué Hay en Mi Escritorio? A Supply Memory Game
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: You know the seven words and you can follow the commands. Now test your memory: a handful of supplies on a desk, ten seconds to look, then everything gets covered — and you name what you saw, in Spanish.

To say what is on the desk, start with hay, which means 'there is' or 'there are.' You already used it for counting last week: 'Hay veinte estudiantes en mi clase.' It works the same way for objects:

En el escritorio hay un cuaderno. — On the desk there is a notebook.
Hay una regla y un bolígrafo. — There is a ruler and a pen.

The word for 'a' matches the noun's group, the same el/la match you learned on Monday: un for the el words (un cuaderno, un bolígrafo, un borrador), una for the la words (una regla, una pizarra, una computadora). And when there is more than one, add -s just like in English: un cuaderno, dos cuadernos; una regla, tres reglas.

Here is the memory game:

1. One player puts four or five real supplies on a desk or tray — maybe a cuaderno, a regla, two bolígrafos, and a borrador.
2. Everyone looks for ten seconds. Then the player covers the tray with a cloth or a jacket.
3. Take turns naming one thing that was there: 'Hay un cuaderno.' 'Hay dos bolígrafos.' Use last week's numbers whenever there is more than one.
4. Uncover and check. Add one more object each round to make it harder.

You just held a whole desktop of Spanish words in your head and named them from memory, counting the ones that came in pairs. Tomorrow you switch from listening to reading: a written instruction card with four steps to follow — draw, write, and cut.

objectives: Recall the seven supply names from memory after a brief look
Say what is on a desk using the frame hay + un/una + noun
Use last week's numbers with plural supplies (dos bolígrafos, tres reglas)
materialsNeeded: Four to six real classroom supplies and a cloth or jacket to cover them
A family member or classmate to play with
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review the seven words from Monday quickly, articles included.
2. Introduce hay ('there is / there are'), connecting it to last week's 'Hay veinte estudiantes.'
3. Show the un/una match: un for el words, una for la words. Practice a few: un cuaderno, una regla, un borrador, una computadora.
4. Point out the -s plural and pair it with numbers: dos cuadernos, tres reglas.
5. Play the memory game: set out 4-5 supplies, look for ten seconds, cover, take turns saying 'Hay un/una...' or 'Hay dos/tres...'. Add an object each round.
6. Play the speed-drill activity.
7. Complete the worksheet.
8. Preview tomorrow's written instruction card.
differentiationTips: Struggling: keep every round to single objects so the child only has to produce 'Hay un cuaderno' without adding numbers
Ready for more: use six or seven objects with several repeats, so the child must say 'Hay cuatro bolígrafos' and get both the number and the -s ending right
For the teaching adult: un/una is the indefinite article ('a / an'); the child does not need that label, just the el-word / la-word match. Plural agreement beyond adding -s is not a week 6 target
This game is a live spoken exchange, so it does not depend on the audio-recording gap noted elsewhere (open decision, expansion-plan-2026-09.md §12.9)
teacherGuide.answerKey: Frame: hay = 'there is / there are.' Use un with el words (un cuaderno, un bolígrafo, un escritorio, un borrador) and una with la words (una regla, una pizarra, una computadora). Plurals add -s and pair with numbers: dos cuadernos, tres reglas, cuatro bolígrafos. Speed-drill answers are the seven words with articles: el cuaderno, el bolígrafo, la regla, el escritorio, la pizarra, el borrador, la computadora.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: The scope-and-sequence names a 'What's on my desk?' memory game as the Day 3 activity. Recalling and naming supplies under a memory load exercises the productive edge of the week's WA-WL-2015.1.2 work, while the hay + un/una frame gives the child a reusable sentence shape rather than isolated words. Folding last week's numbers into the plural counts is the deliberate spiraling the course's band notes call for, keeping numbers 0-100 active while the new vocabulary lands.
